The task of these decision support systems is often to estimate the model parameters and use them to suggest the best option. For example, financial services firms use decision support systems to assist with loan and mortgage payouts, wealth and asset management, investment and retirement planning, financial consultation, and credit risk assessment. The task of these decision support systems is often to estimate the model parameters and use them to suggest the best option. Since financial decisions are often very sensitive for consumers and mistakes can carry a huge cost for the consumer, these systems take the form of decision engines with decision support capabilities to flag likely bad decisions for consumers. Hence, the consequences of the output of these engines, in areas such as loan rejection or mortgage denial, can often have a large impact.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.70593/978-93-49910-91-1_9\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 6, 10]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Determining Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence-Based Security Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The chapter discusses the determination of who is responsible when artificial intelligence is used for security decision making within complex organizational environments. It looks at how accountability is shared among system designers, vendors, deployers, and human operators when AI-driven tools are used to influence detection actions, prioritization, and response. The chapter investigates legal principles explaining the relationship between control, foreseeability, and duty of care, along with regulatory requirements for human oversight and governance. It also examines issues related to automation bias, black-box models, and extended decision chains that involve Security Operations Centers and third parties. Special focus is given to documentation, role clarity, chain of command for escalation, and auditability as means of defining responsibility. Through combining a legal perspective with security operational practice, the chapter outlines a system for determining responsibility, handling liability, and making defensible decisions in AI-assisted security systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 9]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "94c61e216b83acd2862dd18e8a35e5759f5d74006c45eb0b8960f659a0e75944", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.22381/sg2320234", "doi:10.4337/9781803926216.00024", "doi:10.70593/978-93-49910-91-1_9", "doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.22381/sg2320234", "https://doi.org/10.4337/9781803926216.00024", "https://doi.org/10.70593/978-93-49910-91-1_9", "https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
